Ana, I have eight minutes. Can we sign the master agreement this week, what does clause nine actually say, and do I need to give the board a heads-up?

Three answers. We should not sign this week. Clause nine provides that our liability is capped at one month of fees. And yes — give them a heads-up today, because the sticking point is the cap, not the turnaround.
Their counsel told me on Friday they agreed to raise it. And what is an affiliate, by the way? The board will ask.

They proposed raising it. Nothing has been agreed, and it is not in the wording. And an affiliate is a company that belongs to the same group as the counterparty — which matters here, because the cap covers them too.
Fine. And if I sign it as it stands on Friday, how bad is it?
If we sign it as it stands, we carry the whole exposure above one month of fees. My recommendation is to hold until we have their buy-in in writing. Expect pushback on the timing, not on the cap.

I work with lawyers in six countries, and I can tell you the exact moment a lawyer stops being hard work. It is not when the accent improves. It is when they stop translating. In the first months you ask a simple question and you can hear the machine: they take what you asked, turn it into their own language, find the answer, and build it back in English. Two seconds of silence, then a long sentence that answers something slightly different. Now compare that with the ones who have been at it a while. I ask whether we can sign, and I get an obligation back: we should not, until this is fixed. I ask what the clause says, and I get one line, in the present tense. I ask how bad it would be, and I get a condition, not a story. Same person, same accent, half the words. That is what I call fluent. Not the sound. The fact that every question comes back in the shape it was asked in, and I can act on the answer without booking a second call.

When I started a program like this one, I expected my English to get more beautiful. Longer sentences, better words, the kind of English you read in a judgment. That is not what happened. What happened is that it got shorter. My first summaries were three paragraphs and everybody still asked me what I meant. My summaries now are four lines, and nobody asks anything. Somewhere around the ninth or tenth week I noticed that I had stopped building sentences. I was choosing. Somebody asked me a question, and before I opened my mouth I already knew: this one is a condition, this one is only reporting the document, this one needs the passive because it is not about who made the mistake. It became a decision, not a translation. And I should be honest about what still catches me. Anything I did not prepare for, and an accent I have never heard before. Those two still take everything I have. But now I know what to say while I buy myself the time, and nine weeks ago I did not.

Here is a quick heads-up: the amendment will not be ready this week. The sticking point is the liability cap, not the turnaround. They proposed a workaround on the call, but nothing has been agreed. So my recommendation is to hold until we have their buy-in in writing.
